_comment: Shipped defaults. Do not edit this file -- it documents the full schema and is the
reference the validator checks against. Put your overrides in config.json, which is
deep-merged on top of this (objects merge; arrays REPLACE, so you can remove a default
STUN server rather than only add to it). Secrets belong in environment variables, not
in a JSON file that might get shared: see the STREAMER_* overrides in docs/SETUP.md.
The quality preset ladder is NOT here. It lives in public/shared/quality-math.js so the
browser and the server read the identical definitions; duplicating it into config would
create a second source of truth for the numbers the encoder is driven by.

_hostComment: The host role survives an accidental reload: on socket loss a grace timer runs, and a
rejoin carrying the matching hostToken reclaims it. Reclaim is evaluated on the join
itself, not on a janitor tick, so the deadline is exact.
A host who clicks Leave is promoting immediately -- the grace window exists for
unexpected socket loss, not for a deliberate exit, and waiting 30s would leave the room
with nobody able to end the session.
emptyRoomGraceMs MUST exceed hostGraceMs, and the validator enforces it: a solo host's
own reload empties the room, and if empty-room cleanup ran first the room would be
deleted before the page finished loading, making the whole reclaim mechanism dead code.

_iceComment: STUN is a third party by design: each browser sends UDP binding requests to these
servers, which discloses its public IP and the session timing to whoever runs them.
That is the cost of discovering your own address behind NAT. Set iceServers to [] for
a LAN-only deployment, where host candidates connect without any of this.
TURN is off by default because enabling it routes media through a relay -- the one
thing this app otherwise never does.
_turnComment: A relay for the cases STUN cannot solve. Direct connection fails when both ends sit
behind symmetric NAT, and no configuration on either machine can change that -- it is a
property of the networks in between.
Disabled by default, and that is the important part: enabling it routes media through a
third party, which is the one thing this app otherwise never does. It is here so that a
call which will not connect is a one-flag fix rather than an evening of debugging, not
The urls below are Metered's Open Relay, which is free and needs no signup. Its
credentials are public and shared, so treat it as best-effort: its operator can see that
a session happened and how much data moved, never its contents -- media stays end-to-end
encrypted even when relayed. If you need this regularly, run coturn on a machine you own
(Oracle Cloud's always-free tier is enough) and put its address here instead.
iceTransportPolicy stays 'all' so the relay is a fallback, not the default path: ICE
only uses it when nothing direct works. Setting 'relay' would force every call through

_presetComment: The preset sets the CEILING -- resolution, frame rate, bitrate. How those bits are spent
is decided separately, from what the capture is actually doing, because a shared screen
is two different problems wearing one name.
A code editor or a document is a still picture. A desktop capturer only emits frames that
CHANGED, so such a surface produces 1-3 fps whatever the preset asks for, and a 'motion'
hint then spends the whole bitrate protecting a frame rate nobody is producing -- paid
for in the one currency the viewer can see. Measured in the field: 1728x1080 arriving at
2 fps and 47 kbps, soft in every direction. Video or a game is the opposite.
So the app watches media-source.framesPerSecond (the CAPTURER's rate, not the encoder's)
and switches contentHint between 'detail' and 'motion' with hysteresis. See
trackContentMode in public/shared/quality-math.js. That is why the default can stay at
the top of the ladder: it no longer forces one answer onto both kinds of content.
_budgetComment: Total outbound video budget, divided by the number of REMOTE peers you send to
(participants - 1), never by the participant count. At the default 4-participant cap
that is 20000/3 = 6.67 Mbps per peer, which is what makes the 1080p60 default (6 Mbps)
reachable. The two numbers were chosen together.
20 Mbps is a LAN or fibre figure. On residential upstream -- often 1-5 Mbps -- it is
far above the real link, which makes the clamp inert exactly where it was meant to
help: the encoder saturates the uplink and takes the signaling socket and the audio
down with it until adaptation reacts. Two mitigations, both on by default: the lobby
exposes this as an editable 'Your upload speed', and bandwidth-triggered step-downs
use a shorter window than CPU-triggered ones so saturation is measured in seconds.
Set it to your actual measured upload speed. It is the single most useful number to
The default is 10000 rather than 20000 because 20 Mbps was an aspiration, not a
measurement, and a budget above the real link is worse than no budget: it makes the
clamp inert precisely where it was supposed to help. 10 Mbps is a defensible figure
for ordinary home fibre, and it still leaves the whole budget to the single remote
peer in a two-person call -- enough for the 1080p60 default at 6 Mbps.
_adaptComment: Consecutive 1-second samples of a limitation reason before stepping down one rung.
Bandwidth reacts faster than CPU because a saturated uplink degrades everything on the
link, including the WebSocket; a busy CPU only degrades the video.
Raising is never automatic -- the UI suggests it and the user decides.
adaptWarmupMs ignores everything for the first seconds of a new video track. During
that window the encoder is still ramping and the send rate is legitimately far below
the cap while qualityLimitationReason reads 'bandwidth' -- the estimator probing, not
congestion. Adapting on it permanently downgrades a call that was about to be healthy.
Measured here, a 1080p60 share climbed 960x540 -> 1280x720 -> 1920x1080 over about
twelve seconds, reporting 'bandwidth' throughout; 15s clears that with margin. The
primary defence is the availableOutgoingBitrate check in quality.js -- this is the
backstop for browsers that do not report an estimate.

_comment: echoCancellation is ON. It was off originally, on the assumption that everyone wears
headphones -- and that assumption was simply wrong for the people using this. Two
laptops on speakers, with AEC off, means each side hears itself back through the
other side's microphone and there is nothing anywhere to suppress it.
What AEC does NOT do, because it was once changed in the belief that it would: it
processes only the signal you SEND. It cannot stop you hearing your own voice locally
(that is Windows 'Listen to this device' or a headset's sidetone -- see
docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md), and it does nothing for a microphone that delivers silence.
The cost is real: AEC processes the shared system audio too, so music and video you
share lose some fidelity. That is a worse trade than an unusable call. Set it to false
if everyone is on headphones and you are sharing media where the difference matters.
It can also be toggled per session from the microphone menu in the room.
stdout only, never a file. SDP and ICE candidates are never logged even at debug: they
contain network topology, and this app has no reason to retain any of it.
